subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Guard cells open the stomata when they:
options: Are exposed to darkness
Lose water and become flaccid
Lose potassium ions to neighbouring cells
Accumulate solutes, take up water by osmosis and become turgid
questions.explain: Active uptake of K+ lowers guard-cell water potential, so water enters by osmosis; the cells become turgid and bend apart, opening the pore.

questions.q: The semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves open when:
options: Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
Ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery
The AV valves are also open
The ventricles relax during diastole
questions.explain: Once ventricular pressure rises above arterial pressure the semilunar valves open and blood is ejected.

questions.q: Directional selection is characterised by:
options: The mean phenotype being favoured
No change in allele frequencies
Both extremes being favoured over the mean
The population mean shifting towards one extreme phenotype
questions.explain: Directional selection favours one extreme, shifting the population mean in that direction over time.

questions.q: As an organism increases in size, why does it require a specialised exchange surface?
options: Volume increases more slowly than surface area
Larger cells respire anaerobically and need no oxygen
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio decreases, so diffusion across the body surface cannot meet metabolic demand
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio increases, slowing diffusion
questions.explain: As size increases, volume rises faster than surface area, so the SA:V ratio falls and the body surface alone cannot supply the cells.

questions.q: In the mark-release-recapture method, the Lincoln index estimates population size N using which expression?
options: N = (first marked + second sample) / 2
N = recaptured marked / (first marked x second sample)
N = (first marked x second sample) / recaptured marked
N = first marked + second sample - recaptured marked
questions.explain: Population = (number first marked x total in second sample) / number marked in the second sample.

questions.q: Reproductive isolation is essential for speciation because it:
options: Removes natural selection
Prevents gene flow between diverging populations so they accumulate genetic differences
Increases mutation rates
Forces all individuals to interbreed
questions.explain: Without gene flow, populations diverge genetically until they can no longer interbreed, becoming separate species.

questions.q: What is the function of the non-conducting (fibrous) tissue between the atria and ventricles?
options: To delay and channel the impulse through the AVN so the ventricles contract after the atria
To prevent blood entering the ventricles
To speed conduction directly from atria to ventricles
To act as a second pacemaker
questions.explain: The fibrous ring stops the impulse passing directly to the ventricles, forcing it through the AVN, ensuring atria empty before ventricles contract.

questions.q: In the biological species concept, two organisms belong to the same species if they can:
options: Interbreed to produce fertile offspring
Share any DNA sequence
Look physically similar
Live in the same habitat
questions.explain: The biological species concept defines a species as a group able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

questions.q: The maximum population size an environment can support sustainably is known as the:
options: Carrying capacity
Limiting factor
Climax population
Biotic potential
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the maximum population an ecosystem's resources can support over a long period.

questions.q: Stabilising selection acts to:
options: Favour both extremes against the mean
Increase the mutation rate
Favour one extreme phenotype
Favour the intermediate (mean) phenotype and reduce variation
questions.explain: Stabilising selection favours the mean phenotype, selecting against extremes and reducing variation.

questions.q: Human birth mass shows that very small and very large babies have higher mortality, while intermediate masses survive best. This illustrates:
options: Sexual selection
Disruptive selection
Directional selection
Stabilising selection
questions.explain: Selection against both extremes in favour of the intermediate is stabilising selection.

questions.q: A crop fixes 30,000 kJ per m2 per yr (NPP). A primary consumer assimilates 4,500 kJ per m2 per yr. What is the percentage efficiency of energy transfer?
Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are reproductively isolated by:
options: A geographical barrier such as a mountain or river
A behavioural difference within the same area
Polyploidy
A change in mating season only
questions.explain: In allopatric speciation a physical/geographical barrier separates populations, allowing them to diverge.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 1 in 100 individuals is homozygous recessive. The frequency of the recessive allele (q) is:
questions.explain: q squared = 0.01, so q = the square root of 0.01 = 0.1.

questions.q: The chloride shift refers to:
options: The exchange of oxygen for chloride at the alveoli
The loss of Cl- from plasma during digestion
The active uptake of chloride during the Bohr effect
The movement of Cl- into red blood cells to balance the charge as HCO3- leaves
questions.explain: As hydrogencarbonate ions diffuse out of red cells, chloride ions move in to maintain electrical neutrality.

questions.q: Which factor would DECREASE the rate of transpiration from a leaf?
options: A rise in temperature
A decrease in atmospheric humidity
An increase in air movement (wind)
An increase in atmospheric humidity
questions.explain: Higher humidity reduces the water-potential gradient between the leaf air spaces and the atmosphere, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.

questions.q: During succession, how does each community typically change the environment?
options: It removes all soil
It makes conditions less suitable for itself but more suitable for the next community
It prevents any further change
It reduces biodiversity at every stage
questions.explain: Each stage alters the abiotic conditions, often making them less suitable for itself but enabling new species to colonise.

questions.q: What is a deflected succession (plagioclimax)?
options: A succession that reaches its natural climax community
A community held at a stage before the natural climax by human activity such as grazing
The earliest pioneer stage of succession
A succession occurring entirely underwater
questions.explain: Continued human or animal interference, such as grazing or mowing, stops succession reaching its natural climax.

questions.q: During atrial systole, blood moves from the atria into the ventricles because:
options: The atria relax and fill with blood
The semilunar valves open
Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
Atrial pressure rises above ventricular pressure, pushing the AV valves open
questions.explain: Contraction of the atria raises atrial pressure above that of the ventricles, forcing the open AV valves to allow blood through.

questions.q: Antibiotic resistance spreading through a bacterial population is an example of:
options: Disruptive selection
Stabilising selection
Directional selection
Genetic drift only
questions.explain: The antibiotic shifts the population towards the resistant extreme, a clear case of directional selection.

questions.q: Why is the tracheal system of an insect generally unsuitable for supporting a very large body size?
options: Haemolymph cannot carry any oxygen
Tracheoles fill permanently with fluid in large insects
Diffusion of oxygen along long tracheae becomes too slow to meet demand deep in the body
Spiracles cannot be closed in large insects
questions.explain: Because the system relies largely on diffusion, oxygen cannot reach deep tissues fast enough in a large insect, limiting body size.

questions.q: Insects limit water loss from their tracheal system mainly by:
options: Closing the spiracles using valves and hairs
Producing surfactant in the tracheoles
Increasing ventilation by abdominal pumping
Using haemoglobin to carry oxygen in the blood
questions.explain: Spiracles can be closed by valves, reducing the evaporative water loss that would otherwise occur from the moist tracheal lining.

questions.q: Spongy mesophyll in a leaf is adapted for gas exchange because:
options: It contains many chloroplasts for trapping light
Air spaces between loosely packed cells provide a large moist surface for diffusion
It transports water to the stomata
It actively pumps carbon dioxide into the cells
questions.explain: Loosely packed cells with interconnected air spaces give a large moist surface area, allowing gases to diffuse to and from photosynthesising cells.

questions.q: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a shoot, which is used as an estimate of transpiration. A key assumption is that:
options: Water uptake exactly equals water lost as vapour
The shoot continues to grow during the experiment
No water is used in photosynthesis or stored in cells
Stomata are fully closed throughout
questions.explain: The potometer assumes that virtually all water taken up is lost in transpiration, though a small amount is actually used by the plant.

questions.q: A high value of an index of diversity (e.g. Simpson's index) for a habitat indicates:
options: A single dominant species
Many species each fairly evenly represented
Low resistance to environmental change
Few species and many individuals of one species
questions.explain: A high diversity index reflects many species in relatively even proportions, indicating a more stable ecosystem.

questions.q: The myoglobin dissociation curve lies to the LEFT of the haemoglobin curve, which means myoglobin:
options: Carries four oxygen molecules like haemoglobin
Has a higher affinity for oxygen and acts as an oxygen store in muscle
Cannot bind oxygen at low partial pressures
Releases oxygen at higher partial pressures than haemoglobin
questions.explain: Myoglobin's high oxygen affinity means it only releases oxygen at very low partial pressures, acting as a reserve store in muscle.

questions.q: The founder effect occurs when:
options: A small group establishes a new population carrying only a subset of the original gene pool
A large population is split equally by a barrier
Selection favours heterozygotes
Mutation rate suddenly increases
questions.explain: A few founding individuals carry only part of the parent population's genetic variation, skewing allele frequencies in the new population.

questions.q: On a sigmoid (S-shaped) population growth curve, what does the levelling-off at the top represent?
options: Extinction of the population
The population reaching its carrying capacity
The lag phase
The exponential phase
questions.explain: The plateau represents the carrying capacity, where birth and death rates balance and the population stops growing.

questions.q: In bony fish, the operculum contributes to gas exchange by:
options: Adding oxygen to the water before it reaches the gills
Pumping blood through the gill lamellae
Maintaining a near-continuous flow of water over the gills
Filtering food particles from the water
questions.explain: Coordinated movements of the buccal cavity and operculum keep water flowing over the gills almost continuously, maintaining exchange.

questions.q: During strenuous activity an insect may ventilate its tracheal system more effectively by:
options: Rhythmic abdominal pumping movements that move air through the tracheae
Closing all spiracles to retain oxygen
Switching to cutaneous gas exchange
Increasing the water content of the tracheoles
questions.explain: Abdominal muscle contractions change body volume, mass-flowing air through the tracheae to supplement diffusion during high demand.
